sections.html:
Wood County deeds are recorded by the Recorder, whose suite is upstairs at One Courthouse Square in Bowling Green. You can hand it over in person or send it by post. The phone is 419-354-9140, and the counter is staffed weekdays, 8:30 to 4:30.

A sale passes through three desks. The Recorder holds the lasting record, the Auditor puts the new owner on the tax rolls, and the Treasurer (419-354-9130) is who you ask about unpaid taxes on the parcel. Rentals make up 34.1 percent of occupied homes here, so some of your buyers will be investors.

sections.h2: What makes a deed ready to record
sections.html:
Revised Code 5301.01 asks for the grantor's signature plus a notary's acknowledgment. File in the county holding the land. If you skip filing, Revised Code 5301.25 lets a later good faith buyer with no notice win out over your unrecorded deed.

The office website posts its document standards and explains marginal references. These link a new paper to an earlier one by instrument number or by volume and page, the way a release names the mortgage it cancels. Naming the prior deed inside your deed is free. Naming a land contract or a terminated life estate gets indexed and billed as a reference. Before it goes in the mail, confirm four things:

  • The signature and notary block are complete.
  • The legal description matches the previous recorded deed or a newer survey.
  • The Auditor's endorsement appears on the front.
  • The payment covers each page, including the caption page.

Revised Code 317.32 splits each recording charge into two equal halves, a base fee and a housing trust fund fee. A half costs $17 for pages one and two and $4 for every further page. Counties can tack on a preservation surcharge of up to $5. The Recorder's site includes an estimator that totals the fees for your paperwork.

Pages are eight and a half by fourteen inches, and a partial page is charged in full. A long exhibit therefore costs more.

Recording charges a home seller is most likely to meet
ChargeAmount
Pages one and twoTwo halves of $17 each
Each added pageTwo halves of $4 each
County preservation surchargeCapped at $5
Reference entered by a separate instrumentTwo halves of $2 each, per reference
Copy of a recorded page$2.00 each

sections.h2: Why the Auditor sees the deed first
sections.html:
The transfer is arranged with the Auditor at 419-354-9150. A value statement comes from the buyer, the Auditor marks the fee on the deed, and the stamped paper then goes to the Recorder. The fee under Revised Code 319.54 is one dollar or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is larger. The seller pays. The Auditor shares the Recorder's floor in the County Office Building, so a deed moves between counters without anyone leaving the building.

A board of commissioners can levy its own transfer tax, up to thirty cents per hundred dollars (Revised Code 322.02). Phone the Auditor to learn if one applies, then fold that into your closing estimate.

sections.h2: How to search records or order a copy
sections.html:
The office website has three ways to search.

  • Adaptable Visual Access covers the index from 1980 forward, a day or so after each filing.
  • A Laredo Anywhere account shows images of documents. It is built for heavy professional use, and you must send in an account request form.
  • AmeriScan's Documents-On-Demand shows the old physical book indexes.

Under Revised Code 317.13, every county recorder must post indexes and images of instruments from 1980 onward and accept conveyances electronically. A recorder may not charge a fee just to open a login.

Each copied page is $2.00. Every request needs an instrument number or a book and page, because staff will not dig through a document to find a legal description for you. A typical order runs like this:

  1. Search the index by name and write down the instrument number.
  2. Decide whether you want the whole document or only certain pages. The first or last page needs no extra identification.
  3. Send the number and page choice by email or phone.

sections.h2: From signing to a recorded deed
sections.html:
Skip a stop and the deed comes back to you. This is the usual route.

  1. You sign before a notary, who completes the acknowledgment.
  2. The buyer hands the Auditor a value statement. The Auditor takes the conveyance fee and stamps the front of the deed.
  3. The stamped deed reaches the Recorder along with payment for all pages. It is logged and appears in the index roughly a day later.
  4. The recorded deed is returned, and the Auditor updates the tax rolls to the buyer's name.

A title company normally runs this chain. If you are doing it yourself, phone the Recorder first and confirm the page count and total.

sections.h2: What to bring to the counter
sections.html:
Carry the original signed deed rather than a copy, plus the legal description from your last recorded deed. Should the deed mention an older mortgage, land contract or life estate, have its instrument number or volume and page handy so the reference is indexed properly. Payment must cover every page, caption page included. Run the estimator first so you know the amount, and keep your receipt and the instrument number the office gives you, since you will need that number for any later copy.

For paper format, call the Recorder at 419-354-9140. For the fee stamped on the deed, call the Auditor.

sections.h2: Selling with an old mortgage or lien
sections.html:
Did you pay off a mortgage that never got a recorded release? Request one from the lender and record it with a marginal reference to the original. After that, ask the Treasurer if any tax is still due.

A good habit before listing is to look yourself up in the Recorder's online index and read the instrument that put the house in your name. Compare its legal description with your survey or tax bill. If a name is misspelled or a mortgage release is missing, you will want to learn that now, while there is time to record a correction, and not on the week of closing when a buyer's title agent flags it.

Settle these before listing. Any buyer's title company will turn them up, and each can hold a closing back. A cash purchase has no lender underwriting, yet the title search still happens, so loose mortgages and unpaid taxes need fixing in every case.

Fifteen school systems draw from Wood County, so be ready to say which one serves your address. A parcel near a county line is recorded wherever the land actually sits.

faqs.q: How much is the recording fee for a Wood County deed?
faqs.a: For two pages you pay $17 plus a matching $17 housing trust fund fee. Each extra page adds $4 and $4, and a preservation surcharge of up to $5 may apply. Use the estimator on the Recorder's website for your exact total.

faqs.q: Does Wood County charge a transfer tax on a sale?
faqs.a: Most sales owe the Auditor's conveyance fee, paid by the seller. A separate county transfer tax applies only if commissioners enacted one, so ask the Auditor at 419-354-9150.

faqs.q: Can I order my recorded deed by phone?
faqs.a: Yes. Find the instrument number in the online index and call or email it to the office. Pages are $2.00 apiece.

faqs.q: Do Wood County's online records include old deeds?
faqs.a: The index starts in 1980 and runs about a day behind. Older records are in book indexes served through AmeriScan.

faqs.q: What happens if a signed deed is never recorded?
faqs.a: The buyer carries the risk, because a later good faith purchaser can beat an unrecorded deed. Filing right after closing closes that gap.
